blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

### Development setup

React runs on Vite's dev server, and Spring Boot on another port. Different ports mean different origins, so the browser would apply CORS rules. A **proxy** avoids this in development.

blocks.title: vite.config.ts: forward /api to Spring Boot

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|/ and assets| V[Vite :5173]
  B -->|/api/orders| V
  V -->|proxied| S[Spring Boot :8080]
blocks.title: Same-origin during development

blocks.text:
The browser only sees one origin, so no CORS is involved, and your code can use relative URLs such as `/api/orders`.

### CORS

If the two are on different origins in production, the server must allow it.

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant S as Spring Boot
  B->>S: OPTIONS /api/orders, Origin: https://shop.example.com
  S-->>B: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.example.com
  B->>S: POST /api/orders
  S-->>B: 201, with the allow-origin header
blocks.title: A preflight request
CORS through Spring Security

blocks.text:
Common causes of CORS errors:

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| Works in Postman, fails in the browser | CORS is only enforced by browsers |
| Preflight fails with 401 | Spring Security blocks OPTIONS: enable `.cors()` in the chain |
| `*` with credentials fails | Wildcards can't be used with credentials |
| Header missing only on errors | The error response bypasses your CORS configuration |
| A 500 shown as a CORS error | The real error is hidden: check the server's logs |

### A small API client

Don't scatter `fetch` everywhere. One module handles the base URL, JSON, tokens and errors.

blocks.title: lib/api.ts

blocks.text: Axios is a popular alternative, with interceptors and automatic JSON, though `fetch` is enough for many apps.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Use a proxy in development
- CORS is enforced by browsers
- Centralise API calls
- Check the server logs behind a CORS error

### Options

| Approach | How | XSS risk | CSRF risk | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Server session with HttpOnly cookie | Spring Session; cookie sent automatically | Low | Needs protection | Your own frontend and API, same site |
| JWT in memory, refresh in HttpOnly cookie | Short-lived access token | Lower | For the refresh endpoint | SPA with a separate API |
| JWT in localStorage | Simple | **High** | None | Avoid for sensitive apps |
| Backend for frontend (BFF) | Server holds tokens; browser has a cookie | Low | Needs protection | OAuth with strong security |

Don't assume that JWTs are required: a session cookie is simple and strong when your frontend and API share a site.

### Access and refresh tokens

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as React
  participant A as Spring Boot
  R->>A: POST /login
  A-->>R: Access token in JSON, refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie
  R->>A: GET /orders with Bearer token
  A-->>R: 200
  Note over R,A: 15 minutes later
  R->>A: GET /orders
  A-->>R: 401
  R->>A: POST /refresh (cookie sent automatically)
  A-->>R: New access token
  R->>A: Retry GET /orders
  A-->>R: 200
blocks.title: Refreshing a short-lived access token
A shared refresh, so that parallel 401s don't all refresh

blocks.text:
Ten requests may fail at once, and without this shared promise, ten refreshes run. With refresh token rotation, this can log the user out. Keep this in mind.

### Keeping the user in React

blocks.title: An auth hook on TanStack Query

blocks.text:
Treat `/me` as the source of truth. On logout, call the server, and clear the query cache, so that the next user doesn't see cached data on a shared computer.

### Roles in the UI

Hide buttons a user can't use, for a better experience. But every API call must still check. **Hiding isn't protecting.**

blocks.code: {user.permissions.includes('ORDER_REFUND') && <RefundButton order={order} />}
blocks.title: Show actions by permission

blocks.text:
### Login with Google, using OAuth

For an SPA, use the **Authorization Code flow with PKCE**, or let Spring Boot act as the OAuth client as a backend for frontend, which keeps tokens away from the browser. Avoid the old implicit flow.

**"Where do you store a JWT in the browser?"** Ideally not in localStorage, as XSS can read it. I'd hold a short-lived access token in memory, and a refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, or use a session cookie if the API and app share a site.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- A session cookie is often enough
- Avoid localStorage for tokens
- Refresh once, and share the promise
- The API must always check

sections.title: Handling API results in the UI

blocks.text: ### Pagination with Spring Data

blocks.title: A paged endpoint

blocks.text: Spring's `Page` JSON has `content`, `totalElements` and `totalPages`. Recent Spring versions warn that serialising `PageImpl` directly isn't a stable format, so consider `PagedModel`, or your own response record. Note the cap on `size`: never trust a client's page size.

blocks.title: Pagination in React

blocks.text:
### Every async screen has several states

| State | Show |
|---|---|
| Loading first time | Skeleton, in the page's shape |
| Refreshing | Keep content; a small indicator |
| Empty | A helpful message, and the next action |
| Error | What happened, and a retry |
| Partial | Show what loaded |
| Success | The data |

Forgetting the empty and error states is the most common sign of an inexperienced frontend.

### Errors

Spring Boot supports RFC 9457 **Problem Details**, a standard error format.

blocks.code:
{
  "type": "https://example.com/errors/insufficient-stock",
  "title": "Insufficient stock",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Only 2 items are left.",
  "instance": "/api/orders"
}
blocks.title: A problem response

blocks.text:
| Status | UI behaviour |
|---|---|
| 400, 422 | Show on the form's fields |
| 401 | Refresh, or go to login |
| 403 | "You don't have access" |
| 404 | A not-found page |
| 409 | Explain the conflict; offer a reload |
| 429 | Wait and retry; tell the user |
| 500, 503 | A generic message with a retry and a request ID for support |

Don't show raw server messages or stack traces to users. Do report unexpected errors to a tool such as Sentry.

### Real-time updates

| Technique | Direction | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Polling (`refetchInterval`) | Client asks | Simple status checks |
| Server-sent events | Server to client | Notifications, progress, AI streaming |
| WebSockets (STOMP in Spring) | Both ways | Chat, collaboration |

Start with polling, as it's simple, and works through every proxy. Reach for WebSockets only when you truly need both directions and low latency. WebSockets also need sticky routing, or a broker, when you scale out.

### Timezones and formats

Send UTC from the server (`Instant`), and format in the browser for the user.

blocks.title: Formatting for an Indian user
Key points
blocks.text:
- Cap the page size on the server
- Design all states: loading, empty and error
- Use Problem Details
- Start with polling
### The production build

blocks.code:
npm run build     # creates dist/, with hashed file names
npm run preview   # check it locally
blocks.title: Build

blocks.text:
Hashed names such as `index-8f2a1c.js` let you cache files forever, and each new build gets new names. Only `index.html` must not be cached for long.

### Two ways to deploy

| | Serve from Spring Boot | Separate static hosting |
|---|---|---|
| How | Copy `dist` to `resources/static` | S3 + CloudFront, or similar |
| Origin | Same: no CORS | Same if routed behind one domain |
| Deploy | One artefact | Frontend and backend independently |
| Fit | Small apps, portfolio | Production apps |

blocks.code:
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.github.eirslett</groupId>
  <artifactId>frontend-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>1.15.1</version>
  <configuration>
    <workingDirectory>frontend</workingDirectory>
    <nodeVersion>v22.14.0</nodeVersion>
  </configuration>
  <executions>
    <execution><id>install</id><goals><goal>install-node-and-npm</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>ci</id><goals><goal>npm</goal></goals><configuration><arguments>ci</arguments></configuration></execution>
    <execution><id>build</id><goals><goal>npm</goal></goals><configuration><arguments>run build</arguments></configuration></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
blocks.title: Building React inside the Maven build (frontend-maven-plugin)

blocks.text:
### Configuration

Vite embeds `import.meta.env.VITE_*` values **at build time**, in public JavaScript. Never put secrets there: everything in a frontend bundle is public. Anything secret stays on the server. If you need one build across environments, load `/config.json` at start-up.

### Rolling out

A user may keep an old tab open across a deployment, and then a lazy-loaded chunk it wants may no longer exist. Keep old assets for a while after deploying, and catch chunk-load failures with a prompt to refresh. Old frontend code also keeps calling your API, so keep API changes backward compatible.

### CI

blocks.code:
- run: npm ci
- run: npm run lint
- run: npx tsc --noEmit
- run: npm test -- --run
- run: npm run build
blocks.title: A frontend job

blocks.text: `npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says, unlike `npm install`.
API keys in a React bundle can be read by anyone. Call third-party services through your backend, as Spring Boot can hold the secret.
blocks.title: Everything shipped is public
Key points
blocks.text:
- Hashed assets can be cached for a long time
- Short cache for index.html
- Secrets never go in the bundle
- Old tabs keep calling your API

sections.title: A complete CRUD feature, end to end

blocks.text:
This chapter builds a "notes" feature on both sides, showing how each decision connects.

### The Spring Boot API

blocks.title: Records, validation, and ownership checks

blocks.text:
`PagedModel` gives a stable JSON shape with `content` and a nested `page` object. A version conflict from `@Version` throws `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`, which you can map to a 409 in your `@RestControllerAdvice`.

### Frontend: the data layer

blocks.title: features/notes/notes.api.ts

blocks.text: ### Frontend: hooks

blocks.title: features/notes/useNotes.ts

blocks.text: ### Frontend: the list screen

blocks.title: features/notes/NotesPage.tsx

blocks.text: ### Handling the conflict

blocks.title: Showing a version conflict

blocks.text:
### Checklist: what makes this production-minded

| Concern | Where it's handled |
|---|---|
| Ownership | The service, using the token's subject |
| Validation | Bean Validation on the server; Zod for quick feedback |
| Lost updates | `@Version`, and a 409 in the UI |
| Stale results | Query keys, plus abort signals |
| Shareable state | Search and page in the URL |
| All the states | Loading, error, empty, no matches, placeholder |
| Accessible delete | A label naming each row |

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Build features in layers: API, data, screen
- Keep search and page in the URL
- Map 409 and 400 to useful messages
- The server checks ownership
### Server-sent events from Spring Boot

blocks.title: Pushing order status updates
Connecting events to the query cache

blocks.text:
`EventSource` reconnects by itself, but it can't set an `Authorization` header, so it works best with cookie authentication. With bearer tokens, read the stream with `fetch`, as the AI part's chat hook does.

An in-memory emitter map works for one instance only. With several, publish through Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka, so that the instance holding each connection receives the event.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Order service] --> K[Kafka or Redis Pub/Sub]
  K --> I1[API instance 1]
  K --> I2[API instance 2]
  I1 -->|SSE| B1[Browser]
  I2 -->|SSE| B2[Browser]
blocks.title: Live updates across several instances

blocks.text: ### File uploads through the API

blocks.title: Spring multipart upload
An upload form with a preview

blocks.text: The browser adds `multipart/form-data` with the required boundary. Setting it yourself removes the boundary, and Spring then fails to parse the upload. A shared API client that always sets JSON causes this bug.
blocks.title: Don't set Content-Type for FormData

blocks.text: `URL.createObjectURL` holds memory until revoked, hence the cleanup. For large files, use pre-signed URLs, as your AWS part explains.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- EventSource reconnects, but can't set headers
- Scale SSE with a broker
- Let the browser set multipart headers
- Check file content on the server
### A frontend image

blocks.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY dist /usr/share/nginx/html
blocks.title: Build with Node, serve with Nginx

blocks.text: The final image holds only Nginx and static files, with no Node and no source code. This is the multi-stage build from your Docker guide.

blocks.title: nginx.conf

blocks.text:
Spring Boot needs `server.forward-headers-strategy=native` to trust these forwarded headers, for correct redirects and links.

### Running it all locally

blocks.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: postgres
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: dev
    depends_on: [db]
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports: ["8081:80"]
    depends_on: [backend]
volumes:
  dbdata:
blocks.title: docker-compose.yml

blocks.text: ### Security headers

blocks.title: Useful response headers

blocks.text:
A Content Security Policy is the strongest defence against XSS damage, as it limits which scripts can run. Begin in report-only mode, as a strict policy can break inline scripts and third-party tools. Note that `add_header` in a `location` block replaces those from the parent level, so repeat them or use an include.

### Tracking errors and usage

| Tool type | Gives you |
|---|---|
| Error tracking, such as Sentry | Stack traces per release |
| Real user monitoring | Web Vitals from real devices |
| Product analytics | What people actually use |
| Session replay | Reproduces bugs; handle privacy with care |

Respect privacy: get consent where needed, don't record passwords or personal details, and be honest about what you collect.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Multi-stage build, with only static files in the image
- try_files handles client routes
- Turn off buffering for streams
- CSP limits XSS damage
#### Connecting the two halves

items.question: Why does an API work in Postman but not in React?
items.answer: CORS is only enforced by browsers. The server must allow the page's origin.

items.question: Why can a preflight fail with 401?
items.answer: The security filter blocks OPTIONS, as it has no credentials. Enable CORS in the security chain.

items.question: Why have one API module?
items.answer: Base URL, headers, errors and token handling live in one place.

blocks.text: #### Authentication

items.question: Why do many parallel 401s need special handling?
items.answer: Otherwise each triggers a refresh. Share one refresh promise, and retry afterwards.

items.question: On logout, why clear the React Query cache?
items.answer: Otherwise, the next user on that device could see the previous user's data.

items.question: Is hiding the Refund button enough?
items.answer: No. Someone can call the API directly, so the server must check permission.

blocks.text: #### Handling API results in the UI

items.question: What states must an order list handle besides success?
items.answer: First load, background refresh, empty, and error, ideally with a retry.

items.question: Why should the server cap page size?
items.answer: A client could ask for millions of rows, and overload the database.

items.question: When would you pick server-sent events over WebSockets?
items.answer: When only the server needs to push, such as progress or streaming. It's simpler, and uses plain HTTP.

blocks.text: #### Building and deploying

items.question: Can you hide an API key using a VITE_ environment variable?
items.answer: No. It's built into public JavaScript. Keep the key on the server.

items.question: Users get a chunk load error after a deployment. Why?
items.answer: An old tab requested a file that was removed. Keep old assets for a while, and prompt a refresh.

items.question: What's the difference between npm ci and npm install?
items.answer: `npm ci` installs exactly from the lock file, and fails if it disagrees with package.json. Use it in CI.

blocks.text: #### A complete CRUD feature, end to end

items.question: Why does the delete button's label include the note's title?
items.answer: "Delete" alone is ambiguous for a screen reader in a list. The title identifies the row.

items.question: What protects two tabs from overwriting each other?
items.answer: A version sent with each update. `@Version` rejects stale writes, and the UI shows the 409.

items.question: Why keep a separate draft state from the q in the URL?
items.answer: The input must update on every key, whereas the URL and fetch only change when typing pauses.

blocks.text: #### Live updates and file uploads

items.question: An upload fails with "no multipart boundary". Why?
items.answer: Content-Type was set by hand. Let the browser set it for FormData.

items.question: SSE works locally, but only some users get updates in production. Why?
items.answer: Connections are on different instances, and the emitter map is per instance. Publish through a broker.

items.question: Why revoke an object URL?
items.answer: It keeps the file in memory until released or the page closes.

blocks.text: #### Docker, Nginx and production serving

items.question: Why doesn't the final image contain Node?
items.answer: The build stage produced static files, and Nginx serves them, so the image is smaller and safer.

items.question: What does try_files $uri /index.html do?
items.answer: It serves a real file if one exists, or index.html, so that React Router handles the path.

items.question: Why serve the API through the same Nginx?
items.answer: Same origin means no CORS, and only one public address.
